parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: independence of horizontal and vertical motion
hints: Hint 1: Think about which direction controls how long the ball stays in the air - horizontally there is no acceleration, so the horizontal speed stays constant all the way to landing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Horizontal From Vertical**
You can treat horizontal and vertical motion completely separately. Vertically the ball accelerates, but horizontally with no air resistance there is no force, so horizontal velocity stays at $4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Use Constant Speed Horizontally**
For constant speed, $$s = vt$$ so $$t = s/v$$ Convert $180\text{ cm} = 1.80\text{ m}$, then $$t = 1.80 / 4.9 = 0.367\text{ s} \approx 0.37\text{ s}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: v = u + at for vertical component
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on the vertical motion now - what was the starting vertical speed when projected horizontally, and what is the vertical acceleration?
Hint 2: Link that initial speed, acceleration $g$ and your time from (a)(i) with a uniformly accelerated motion equation to get the final vertical speed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up Vertical Motion**
Projected horizontally means initial vertical velocity $u_v = 0$. Vertical acceleration is $a = g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards, acting for time $t = 0.37\text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Calculate Final Vertical Velocity**
Use $$v = u + at$$ vertically: $$v_v = 0 + 9.81 \times 0.367$$ $$v_v \approx 3.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ directed vertically downwards.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: At impact you now have two velocities at right angles - constant horizontal $4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the vertical value from (a)(ii) - sketch them as a right-angled triangle.
Hint 2: Think about which rule combines perpendicular vectors into a resultant magnitude.
Hint 3: Think about which trig ratio links the opposite and adjacent sides of that triangle to give the angle below the horizontal.
parts.proper_answer: magnitude $v = \sqrt{4.9^2 + 3.6^2} = 6.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, angle $\theta = \tan^{-1}(3.6/4.9) = 36^{\circ}$ below horizontal
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine Perpendicular Components**
Horizontal $v_h = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and vertical $v_v = 3.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ are perpendicular. The resultant speed is the hypotenuse: $$v^2 = v_h^2 + v_v^2$$ $$v = \sqrt{4.9^2 + 3.6^2} = \sqrt{24.01 + 12.96} \approx 6.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Find Direction**
The angle $\theta$ below the horizontal satisfies: $$\tan \theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{v_v}{v_h}$$ $$\theta = \tan^{-1}(3.6/4.9) \approx 36^{\circ}$$ So the ball hits at $6.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $36^{\circ}$ to the horizontal.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what density means in terms of mass and volume, and identify the mass and the shape data you are given.
Hint 2: Think about how to get the volume of a solid sphere from its diameter - be careful to halve to get radius and keep metres.
Hint 3: Combine the two ideas to calculate mass divided by that spherical volume.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write Density Definition**
Density is mass per unit volume: $$\rho = m/V$$ Here $m = 0.017\text{ kg}$.

Step 2: **Calculate Sphere Volume**
For a sphere $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$ Diameter $= 0.016\text{ m}$, so radius $r = 0.0080\text{ m}$. $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \times (0.0080)^3 \approx 2.14 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$$

Step 3: **Divide To Get Density**
$$\rho = 0.017 / 2.14 \times 10^{-6} \approx 7900\text{ kg m}^{-3}$$ This is a typical value for steel, which is reassuring.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: conservation of energy spring to ball
hints: Hint 1: Since all the stored elastic energy becomes movement energy, think about which kinetic energy formula uses the mass and launch speed you know.
Hint 2: Substitute $m = 0.017\text{ kg}$ and $v = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and check the value rounds to $0.20\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equate Energies**
Maximum elastic potential energy in the spring $=$ kinetic energy given to the ball, because the track is frictionless and transfer is complete.

Step 2: **Calculate Kinetic Energy**
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ $$E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.017 \times (4.9)^2 = 0.5 \times 0.017 \times 24.01 \approx 0.204\text{ J}$$ This confirms $0.20\text{ J}$ to two significant figures.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember that for a spring obeying Hooke's law, $F = kx$, so $k$ is the steepness of the $F$ against $x$ straight line.
Hint 2: Pick a large, easy-to-read point on the line in Fig. 2.4, convert $x$ from cm to m, then divide $F$ by $x$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Gradient of F-x Graph**
Hooke's law $F = kx$ means $$k = F/x$$ which is the gradient of the straight line through the origin.

Step 2: **Read Off Values**
Take for example $F = 6.4\text{ N}$ at $x = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}$. $$k = 6.4 / 0.10 = 64\text{ N m}^{-1}$$ Any large triangle gives $63$ to $65\text{ N m}^{-1}$. Remember to convert cm to m or $k$ will be 100 times too small.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which elastic energy formula connects the known energy $0.20\text{ J}$, your $k$ from (b)(iii) and the unknown compression $x_0$.
Hint 2: Rearrange that relation to make $x_0$ the subject before putting numbers in, remembering $x_0$ will come out in metres.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write Elastic Energy**
Stored energy is $$E = \frac{1}{2}k x_0^2$$ This is also the area under the $F$-$x$ graph up to $x_0$.

Step 2: **Rearrange and Substitute**
$$x_0 = \sqrt{2E/k}$$ $$x_0 = \sqrt{(2 \times 0.20)/64} = \sqrt{0.00625} \approx 0.079\text{ m}$$ About $7.9\text{ cm}$ compression, consistent with Fig. 2.4.

parts.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: effect of mass on speed for fixed energy
hints: Hint 1: The spring compression is the same, so the stored energy is the same - think about how that fixed energy is shared as $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ when $m$ is now much smaller.
parts.proper_answer: Same compression gives same elastic potential energy, so same kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$. With smaller mass, $v$ must be greater.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Same Energy, Smaller Mass Means Larger Speed**
Compression $x_0$ is unchanged so elastic energy $\frac{1}{2}k x_0^2$ is unchanged. All becomes kinetic $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$. For fixed $E$, $$v = \sqrt{2E/m}$$ A much smaller $m$ gives a much larger $v$. Equivalently, the same average spring force on a smaller mass gives greater acceleration and so greater exit speed.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think vertically after launch - gravity pulls down but air resistance now pushes up significantly on the light ball, so what happens to the resultant downward force and acceleration?
parts.proper_answer: Air resistance acts upward, reducing the resultant vertical force and vertical acceleration, so the ball takes longer to fall to the ground.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Air Drag Reduces Downward Acceleration**
For the light polystyrene ball, weight is small so air resistance is no longer negligible compared to weight. Upward drag subtracts from weight, giving a smaller resultant downward force and hence smaller vertical acceleration than $g$. With less downward acceleration it gains vertical speed more slowly and takes longer to reach the ground.
